title: Nuh's prayer for his parents
hookLine: my Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house believing (71:28)

lines: HOW A LONG LIFE IS SUMMED UP.
THE LAST WORDS START AT HOME.
cards: A long life usually gets summed up in a few words: a eulogy, a last letter, something said from a hospital bed. Nuh's life in the Qur'an is very long.
Surah al-'Ankabut says he stayed among his people nine hundred and fifty years. He preached, they mocked, he built, the flood came. His own son refused to board and was lost in the waves.
And at the very end of the surah that bears his name, the last thing he says is a prayer, and it starts at home.

teach.b: Verse twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Forgive me and my parents and him who entereth my house believing, and believing men and believing women." Look at the shape.
It moves outward like rings in a pond. Me. My parents.
Whoever comes into my house believing. Then every believing man and woman, everywhere, in every time.
The first ring is himself. A prophet, after all those years, still begins: forgive me. In the Qur'an's telling, asking forgiveness isn't only for the wicked; even a prophet asks, right to the end.
The second ring is his parents. The Qur'an doesn't give their names or their story; some commentators took his prayer for them to mean they were believers. And Nuh isn't alone in praying for parents.
Ibrahim prays: my Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the day the reckoning is set up.

In surah al-Isra', children are taught to say: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they cared for me when I was small. Some Muslims say these prayers daily, in the sitting part of the prayer or after it.

Then the circle widens: anyone who walks through his door in faith, then the whole community of believers, people Nuh would never meet. Nuh's family life was not easy; the Qur'an is honest about that.
And still, his last recorded words make room for his parents and for strangers in one breath.

how: Some Muslims pray for their parents daily with the Qur'anic prayers of Nuh (71:28), Ibrahim (14:41) and 17:24, said in the sitting part of the prayer or after it; praying for parents who have died is a familiar act of devotion.

o: a prayer said for parents after they die
the ark Noah built before the flood came
Noah, whose last words pray for his parents

s: the Qur'an gives the names of Nuh's parents
it doesn't tell their names or story.

games.q: nine hundred and fifty years of preaching are over. Nuh prays one last prayer. who does he name first?
games.why: himself: my Lord, forgive me. then his parents, then whoever enters his house believing, then all believers.

practice: If you pray, say Nuh's words slowly a few times: my Lord, forgive me and my parents.
If you don't, bring your parents to mind as they are or as they were; if that relationship is hard, or they've died, hold them gently, at whatever distance you need.
Then let the circle widen to your home, the people who come through your door, and people you'll never meet.

wordCard.voice: Nuh. In 71:28 his last recorded words widen in rings: forgive me, my parents, whoever enters my house believing, and all believers. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive me and my parents. The circle starts at home and keeps widening. Day six hundred forty-nine.
